lines.text: Beverages — or drinks — are an essential part of daily life, social gatherings, and cultural traditions. Water is the most fundamental drink, available as still (flat) or sparkling (fizzy). Hot beverages dominate morning routines: coffee — from a simple black coffee to elaborate lattes, cappuccinos, and espressos — fuels millions of people daily. Tea is equally global, ranging from classic black tea and green tea to herbal infusions like chamomile, peppermint, and ginger tea. Hot chocolate provides a comforting alternative in cold weather. Soft drinks include fizzy drinks (carbonated beverages) like cola and lemonade, as well as fruit juices — orange juice, apple juice, and tropical blends. Smoothies, made from blended fruit and yoghurt, have become a health-conscious favourite. Energy drinks and sports drinks target active consumers. Milk — whether cow's, oat, almond, or soya — is both a drink and a cooking ingredient. Alcoholic beverages form their own vast category, though many people choose non-alcoholic alternatives. Understanding beverage vocabulary is essential for ordering in cafés and restaurants, shopping in supermarkets, reading menus, and discussing preferences — skills that arise in almost every social and professional situation in English.

lines.text: Tea is central to British identity. 'Put the kettle on' is an invitation for a chat. 'Builder's tea' is strong, milky tea. 'Afternoon tea' (with scones and sandwiches) is a formal tradition. 'Cuppa' is slang for a cup of tea. 'Milk first or after?' is a genuine debate.

lines.text: Modern coffee shop terms: 'espresso' (concentrated shot), 'americano' (espresso + water), 'latte' (espresso + steamed milk), 'cappuccino' (espresso + foam), 'flat white' (espresso + microfoam), 'macchiato' (espresso + dot of foam). 'Barista' = coffee maker.

lines.text: Fizzy Drinks: UK vs US Terms
lines.name: Fizzy Drinks: UK vs US Terms

lines.text: 'Fizzy drink' or 'soft drink' (UK) = 'soda' or 'pop' (US). 'Lemonade' in the UK is a clear, carbonated drink; in the US it's flat and made from real lemons. These differences can cause genuine confusion when ordering.
lines.name: 'Fizzy drink' or 'soft drink' (UK) = 'soda' or 'pop' (US). 'Lemonade' in the UK is a clear, carbonated drink; in the US it's flat and made from real lemons. These differences can cause genuine confusion when ordering.

lines.text: UK sizes: small, regular, large. US chains (Starbucks): Tall, Grande, Venti. 'A pint' is both a unit of measure (568ml UK / 473ml US) and a way of ordering beer. 'A shot' of espresso = about 30ml.

lines.text: English has growing vocabulary for non-alcoholic drinks: 'mocktail' (cocktail without alcohol), 'alcohol-free', 'low-alcohol', 'virgin' (e.g. 'virgin mojito'). 'Designated driver' is someone who doesn't drink to drive others home safely.
